caption_cues.text:
Welcome to the data center infrastructure
that keeps the digital world

running. In this lesson, we'll explore the
key physical

components at a high level that make a
data center function: power,

cooling, and layout. Let's imagine a data
center building

and dissect the key components from the
outside in. The first

layers include power and cooling
facilities. We'll start with power.

Data centers have powerful energy systems
designed to keep operations running
24/7, 365 days a year. From

generators and UPSes, batteries, to
distribution switchgear,

the power infrastructure is a critical
system that supplies energy to all the

equipment in the data center. Now on to
the cooling infrastructure.

Chillers, condensers, and air handling
units that help manage temperature

and humidity on the data center floor so
that the systems don't

overheat or shut down. These systems don't
work in

isolation. Every part of the data center
is connected through cables,

power rails, busways, and energy
management systems. They

ensure that power is delivered efficiently
to the rack. Then

comes rack level distribution. This is
where the

actual compute happens, and a lot of the
energy is consumed and heat is

generated. Servers are arranged in
enclosures where hot and cold

air is separated. Cooling via localized
air or liquid

is constantly monitored with smart sensors
and software. All

of this is maintained and monitored by
systems that

control real-time adjustments, alarm, and
automation.

Think of it as the nervous center of the
data center. In the

next lesson, we'll go deeper into specific
subsystems like power and

cooling, but now you should have a
bird's-eye view of how all

the parts come together to create an
always-on environment.

caption_cues.text:
So, now that you understand how data
drives the digital world,

let's answer the big question. What
exactly is a data

center? In simple terms, a data center is
a specialized

facility that houses computing systems,
servers, storage,

and networking hardware. These systems
support everything

from websites and cloud services to
enterprise apps, financial

transactions, and even the AI models we
work with.

You can think of it like this. When you
stream a movie, check your bank

account, join a video call, you're
reaching out to computers

located somewhere in the world inside a
data center.

But a data center is much more than just a
room full of computers.

It's a tightly controlled environment
designed to maximize uptime,

performance, security, all the time being
as

efficient as possible. First, there's
power.

Servers don't just plug into the wall.
Data centers use

redundant power systems. They use backup
generators and

battery arrays to keep everything running
even during outages.

Then there's cooling. Servers compute a
lot of information,
and that generates heat, a lot of it.

So data centers use air and even liquid
cooling systems

to cool server components and maintain
ideal operating

temperatures for these servers to run
reliably and at full speed.

Connectivity is another key layer. Data
centers act as digital

hubs connected to the Internet via high-
speed fiber optic cables.

Many of these are also carrier neutral,
meaning they connect to multiple

providers offering maximum connectivity
options.

Security is baked into every level,
physical and digital. Think of

biometric access, surveillance, and fire
suppression physically.

Firewall segmentation and threat detection
are done digitally

and physically. All together, these
systems

create an environment where critical data
and applications can live safely,
operate continuously, and scale as needed.

But not all data centers are the same.
They vary in size,

purpose, and location. In fact, you can
think of data
centers as existing on a spectrum. Smaller

ones typically serve individual businesses
and enterprises,

while larger ones, hyperscale facilities,
support
vast global cloud platforms. Some
serve small regional businesses. Others,

and they are called hyperscale data
centers, are run by tech giants like

Amazon, Google, or Microsoft, and they
support global
cloud services. Then there are also

edge data centers. They're smaller,
modular units

placed closer to where the data is
generated. These are vital for real-time
services like IoT, 5G, and AI.

Regardless of size, all data centers share
the same goal,

to efficiently process, store, and move
massive
volumes of data reliably, fast, and
securely. So why does this matter? Well,

while we may not see them, data centers
are essential to the

smooth operation of our daily digital
world.

Data centers are the invisible backbone of
everything we do online.

They allow companies to scale, innovate,
and operate globally.

Without data centers, the digital world
simply wouldn't

function. In the next chapter, we'll take
a closer look

inside a data center to explore the key
elements in the physical
infrastructure that powers it all.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a data center in digital infrastructure?

choices.text: To replace the cloud
choices.feedback_incorrect: Cloud services rely on data-center equipment. A facility supports those services rather than replacing the service model.

choices.text: To create mobile apps
choices.feedback_incorrect: Developers create apps. The physical facility provides the equipment and supporting systems on which applications and their services can run.

choices.text: To store and process data through physical hardware
To provide customer support services
choices.feedback_incorrect: Customer support is an organizational function that may use digital services. The data center's underlying role is to house and support the hardware that stores, processes and moves information.

questions.feedback_correct: The data center brings physical computing, storage and networking equipment together with the systems that support its operation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Separate the facility's physical role from the applications or organizational activities it supports.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes cloud computing?

choices.text: A single company-owned data center, regardless of how resources are provided
choices.feedback_incorrect: A single facility can host a private cloud, but ownership and location don't establish the service model. Look for on-demand access to pooled resources.

choices.text: On-demand network access to pooled, configurable computing resources
Any off-site equipment, even when each change requires manual provisioning
choices.feedback_incorrect: Off-site hosting describes location. Cloud also concerns how resources are provisioned, shared and made available on demand.

choices.text: A service that can exist only on the public internet
choices.feedback_incorrect: Private cloud resources can be accessed through private networks. Public internet access is not a requirement for every cloud deployment.

questions.feedback_correct: Cloud describes how computing resources are provided. The physical deployment may vary, and a private cloud need not span many data centers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the resource-delivery characteristics rather than ownership, off-site location or public internet access alone.

to mind? Maybe a secure

building with rows of servers glowing in
green light. That's not wrong,

but it's only the surface. Data centers
are engineered

ecosystems optimized for nonstop digital
operations.

In this video, we'll take a look at how
they're physically structured from

the ground up. The first thing to
understand is that

everything in a data center is built for
maximum uptime. Whether you're

streaming a video, sending an email, or
just using cloud

applications somewhere, a data center is
powering that

experience. To stay online twenty-four
seven,

a data center needs three core systems,
and they all work together.
They're power, cooling, and IT equipment.

Let's start with cooling because heat is
one of the biggest

enemies of performance. Data centers
generate a lot

of heat. On the outside, you'll see
industrial-grade chillers,

condensers, and cooling towers. These
systems work

to remove heat from the building through a
mix of air and liquid cold

methods. Inside, air handling units, also
known as CRACs,

Computer Room Air Conditioners, keep
temperatures in check by distributing

cold air across the data hall. For liquid-
cooled servers,

cooling distribution units, or CDUs,
ensure cold

liquid keeps the servers cool. These
systems

often operate in tandem with raised floors
and cold aisle

containments. They also include smart
sensors. Now let's talk

about power. At the heart of any data
center is an incredibly robust

energy system. Power typically enters from
utility

lines from the grid or renewable sources
and runs through medium and low

voltage switchgear. From here, it's fed
via backup
systems, diesel generators, and UPSs, or

uninterruptible power supplies for short.
These are banks of

batteries and help keep the data center
running during

outages or grid instability. Once
stabilized,

power is distributed through PDUs, or
power distribution

units, and sometimes even intelligent
busbars that reduce
complexity in cable routing. All of this

ensures that each server receives
consistent, safe

electricity. The layout of a data center
also

plays a major role. Most are designed with
hot and cold aisle containments

to keep airflow controlled and cooling
efficient. Sensors track

temperature, humidity, and power usage in
real time.

Centralized control systems allow
technicians to automate responses and

optimize system performance remotely.
Increasingly, data

centers are becoming more sustainable.
Some include microgrids,

solar panels, or fuel cell systems to
reduce reliance on

public utilities and carbon output. Rack-
level equipment

has also evolved. Racks are designed not
only for high-density

performance but also for efficient
airflow, liquid cooling,

cable management, and environmental
sensing.

All these systems, cooling, power, and
monitoring, are

coordinated to keep the data center
reliable and secure.

Downtime isn't an option when you're
supporting financial markets, hospitals,

or global communication platforms. So to
summarize,

data centers are more than just rows of
servers.

They are intricately designed
infrastructures combining engineering,
IT, and environmental controls. Each

component, chillers, batteries, busbars,

or

from the hardware.

processor and other components. They

aisles are often used. This technique

two. From a systems view, heat is

events, cooling systems, like IT systems,

choices.text: Monitor cooling airflow
choices.feedback_incorrect: Airflow monitoring uses sensors and management controls. The supply may have its own cooling, but its primary role is electrical conversion.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the Open Rack DC-busbar example taught here?

choices.text: Power-shelf rectifiers convert AC to DC; the rack busbar distributes DC to compatible equipment.
The busbar itself converts AC to DC, so a rectifier is unnecessary.
choices.feedback_incorrect: A busbar is a conductor for distribution. Rectifiers in the power shelf perform the AC-to-DC conversion in this example.

choices.text: Every server connected to the DC busbar still needs an AC-input supply and its own AC power cord.
choices.feedback_incorrect: Compatible DC-fed equipment connects to the rack busbar. It still needs suitable DC regulation, but this path removes the individual server AC power cord.

choices.text: Installing a DC busbar guarantees fault tolerance without checking capacity, protection or redundancy.
choices.feedback_incorrect: The complete design must cover load, protection, failure and maintenance conditions. A busbar alone establishes none of those guarantees.

questions.feedback_correct: The power shelf converts, the busbar distributes and equipment regulates DC further. Fewer individual cords, serviceable modular supplies and pooled capacity are potential benefits of the complete architecture.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Separate three jobs: power-shelf conversion, busbar distribution and equipment voltage regulation. Then evaluate the complete design.

questions.prompt: In the conventional power-path example, what supports equipment while the backup generator starts?

choices.text: Stored energy delivered through the UPS
A generator before it is ready and selected
choices.feedback_incorrect: The generator must become ready and be selected before it supplies this path. Stored energy bridges the transition in the example.

choices.text: Unused mounting positions elsewhere in the rack
choices.feedback_incorrect: Mounting space is a mechanical allocation. It stores no electrical energy and cannot bridge a supply interruption.

choices.text: The aisle containment barrier without an energy source
choices.feedback_incorrect: Containment separates air paths. It provides no electrical supply when the incoming source is lost.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Trace the source transition and distinguish stored energy from a generator that is still starting, physical space or airflow separation.

slides.video_transcript: When we talk about data centers, the server rack is where it all begins. In the same way that a standardized shipping container is a standard form factor for everything we ship in the real world, a server rack is a purpose-built standard form factor for IT equipment. The most common size is a 19-inch rack. The 19-inch rack format has been around for decades, and it remains essential in today's IT infrastructure. The term 19-inch refers to the horizontal width of the rack, specifically the distance between the mounting rails. This is the standard form factor for rack-mountable IT equipment. This standard measurements of 19 inch, which is about 48.2 centimeters, makes it possible to mount a wide variety of servers, switches, patch panels, and other IT equipment, even from different manufacturers, all in the same rack. While the width is standard, it's worth noting that the rack depth can vary on the equipment and use case. Data centers typically use deeper racks to support higher performance or dense compute gear, while shallower depths might be found in edge or telco environments. But racks don't just help with physical space. They're an essential part of organization of equipment, maintenance, airflow management, and security. By vertically stacking equipment in a rack, it helps you save space and keep things manageable. A key measurement you'll often hear is a rack unit or simply a U. One rack unit is 1.75 inches or approximately 44.45 centimeters in height. Most standard racks are 42U tall, meaning they can hold equipment that adds up to about 73.5 inches or roughly 1.87 meters in total height. IT equipment is typically labeled by its U height, like a 1U server or a 2U switch. But in the industry, we don't talk about the physical height in inches or meters unless we are shipping the equipment. Typically, we label the equipment and racks by their U height. The larger the U size, the more capability or function the equipment tends to have, but it also takes up more rack space. Racks are designed to allow for good airflow and front and rear access to all components. This makes maintenance easier and supports good cable management. Neatly routed cables not only look better, they reduce the risk of error and make the airflow more efficient. Speaking of airflow, cooling is built into the design. Equipment sucks cool air from the front and pushes warm air out the back. That's why racks are often arranged in hot and cold aisles. This separation allows facilities to better manage temperature and energy usage. Mounting equipment is done using rails along the sides of the rack. These rails have holes spaced at standard intervals, so equipment can be locked in with screws or quick-release tabs. This keeps everything secure and aligned properly. So why does standardization matter? Well, because it makes it easy to scale. Need to add another server? You know exactly how much rack space you have left and what size fits. That consistency supports both operations and future growth. Now, racks can also have doors, front and rear, that are perforated to allow for airflow, but they also provide security. In summary, a 19-inch rack may seem simple, but it plays a crucial role in the data center. It's the standardized form factor, and it's the backbone of building blocks in the data center. It ensures compatibility, it enables organization, it improves cooling, and it supports security, all while helping scale operations efficiently.

questions.prompt: Which approach puts otherwise rejected data-center heat to productive use?

choices.text: Installing more air vents
choices.feedback_incorrect: Ventilation can change airflow, but extra vents alone do not connect rejected heat to a useful customer.

choices.text: Expanding hard disk usage
choices.feedback_incorrect: Adding storage capacity does not establish a beneficial use for the resulting heat. It can also increase the facility load.

choices.text: Using residual heat to warm nearby communities
Increasing lighting systems
choices.feedback_incorrect: More lighting can increase energy use and heat. Heat reuse instead connects a recoverable source to useful demand.

questions.feedback_correct: Heat reuse can serve a suitable nearby demand. Its value depends on temperature, distance and infrastructure, and it need not lower facility PUE.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for a useful heat customer and the infrastructure needed to deliver suitable heat.

questions.prompt: In data-center energy management, what is a “zombie server”?

choices.text: A backup server that only activates during a system failure
choices.feedback_incorrect: A deliberately maintained standby system can have a required resilience role. It should not be classified as unneeded solely because it is idle.

choices.text: A server that is powered on but no longer doing useful work
A server infected with malware
choices.feedback_incorrect: Zombie can have a malware-related meaning elsewhere. Here the energy-management question concerns equipment consuming power without useful work.

choices.text: A high-performance server running AI workloads
choices.feedback_incorrect: A productive server may consume substantial power while serving a useful workload. High demand alone does not make it a zombie server.

questions.feedback_correct: In this context, the server consumes energy without useful work. Review ownership, dependencies and resilience needs before retiring it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Judge useful work and intended operational role, rather than power level, malware terminology or temporary idleness.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a defensible trend for data-center cooling arrangements?

choices.text: All data centers will be replaced by peer-to-peer devices
choices.feedback_incorrect: Distributed devices still need computing resources and supporting infrastructure. They do not establish that all facilities disappear.

choices.text: Facilities may need both air and liquid cooling for different workloads
All data centers will move into urban high-rise buildings
choices.feedback_incorrect: Site choices depend on workload, resources and constraints. One building form is not a universal destination.

choices.text: One global data center will serve every provider
choices.feedback_incorrect: Latency, resilience, regional requirements and physical capacity create reasons for multiple deployments. A single universal facility is not the supported trend.

questions.feedback_correct: Cooling depends on equipment needs and facility conditions. Mixed air/liquid arrangements can support different workloads.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Choose the workload-dependent arrangement rather than a sweeping claim about every future facility.

term_glossary.tooltip: The rate at which energy is transferred or used. Electrical power is commonly expressed in watts, kilowatts or megawatts.
A quantity accumulated over time. Electrical energy use is commonly expressed in watt-hours or kilowatt-hours.
Additional components or paths that can support a required function when another is unavailable. Shared failure causes still need review.
The ability to remove site infrastructure components or distribution paths for planned maintenance without interrupting the supported operations.
A system's ability to continue proper operation despite specified component failures. The design's failure scope matters.
A facility service in which a customer rents space and contracted supporting infrastructure for its own equipment.
An infrastructure approach designed for very large, repeatable operations and expansion. It describes scale, not one ownership model.
Computing placed close to the users, devices or activity it serves, often to reduce delay or dependence on a distant connection.
Delay between an event or request and the resulting processing, availability or response. Network latency is one contributor to service delay.
A model for on-demand network access to pooled configurable computing resources that can be provisioned and released with little manual effort.
Uninterruptible power supply: a system that supports its connected load through specified supply interruptions, commonly using stored energy while another source becomes available.
Power distribution unit: equipment that distributes electrical power to downstream loads. Facility and rack PDUs differ in scale and features.
Alternating current: electrical current whose direction changes periodically. Conventional facility supplies commonly deliver AC power.
Direct current: electrical current flowing in one direction. Server electronics require DC at their operating voltages; conversion location varies by architecture.
Computer room air conditioner: a room-cooling unit commonly using a compressor and refrigerant circuit. Confirm the actual cooling architecture rather than relying on the label.

Computer room air handler: fans move return air over a chilled-water coil supplied by the facility cooling plant. The air handler has no refrigeration compressor; the water carries heat back to the plant.
Coolant distribution unit: equipment that manages coolant delivery and, in many designs, separates the equipment coolant loop from the facility loop through heat exchange.
A heat-transfer component attached to a hot device, with internal coolant passages that carry heat into a liquid loop.
Physical separation of cold supply air from warm exhaust to reduce mixing and direct airflow through the equipment.
Central processing unit: a processor that executes instructions. Its performance and power needs depend on architecture, configuration and workload.
Random access memory: working memory used by running software. Conventional server RAM is volatile and is distinct from persistent storage.
Graphics processing unit: a processor designed for parallel operations, used for graphics and many accelerated computing workloads.
Solid-state drive: persistent storage using solid-state memory. Endurance, latency, capacity and power vary by product and workload.
Hard disk drive: persistent storage using magnetic media on rotating disks, accessed by mechanical read/write heads.
Non-Volatile Memory Express: specifications for host communication with non-volatile memory across transports such as PCIe and network fabrics; not a physical connector.

RU, also written U, is the conventional rack height unit: 44.45 mm (1.75 in). Open Rack uses OU (OpenU): 48 mm (about 1.89 in). These are different vertical pitches, so 1 RU and 1 OU are not interchangeable. Panel heights allow clearance. Neither unit specifies rack width or depth; equipment needs compatible mounting.

OU, also called OpenU, is the Open Rack vertical equipment pitch: 48 mm (about 1.89 in). A conventional U or RU is 44.45 mm (1.75 in). The two pitches are not interchangeable; verify the rack and equipment mounting standard.
Software abstraction of physical computing resources, allowing separate execution environments to share a physical host. Capacity and isolation still require deliberate management.
A software-defined computing environment with virtual hardware and its own operating system and applications, supported by a hypervisor.
Software that presents virtualized hardware resources to virtual machines and manages their execution and separation on a physical host.
An application execution environment isolated through operating-system mechanisms. Containers typically share the host kernel and need resource and security controls.
Data center infrastructure management: tools used to monitor, model or manage data-center resources such as assets, capacity, power and cooling; capabilities vary by implementation.
Building management system: controls and monitoring for building services, commonly including mechanical and electrical systems. Its scope and integration with DCIM depend on the site.
Power usage effectiveness: total data-center energy divided by IT equipment energy for the same period and defined boundary. It measures facility overhead, not useful computing output.
Water usage effectiveness: water use normalized by IT equipment energy, commonly liters per kilowatt-hour. State the boundary: site water and source water are different measures.
Carbon usage effectiveness: greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to data-center energy divided by IT equipment energy, commonly kg CO₂-equivalent per kWh. State emissions factors and boundaries.
Renewable energy certificate: an instrument representing the renewable attributes of one megawatt-hour of qualifying electricity generation. It does not track physical electrons to a facility.
Power purchase agreement: a contract to purchase electricity under agreed terms. Physical and financial arrangements differ, and renewable-attribute ownership needs separate attention.
In energy management, a powered-on server that performs no useful work. It differs from deliberately reserved standby capacity and needs investigation before removal.
Infrastructure and software organized around developing and running AI at scale; a workload and design lens that can overlap facility ownership, scale and placement categories.
The process of adjusting a model using data.
Using a trained model to produce an output from an input.
OCP project developing open, modular infrastructure approaches for AI beyond hyperscale facilities, including regional, enterprise, telco and industrial environments.
The IT equipment area, including servers, storage and network equipment. Some local power and cooling equipment can also be in this area; a raised floor is not required.
Electrical and mechanical support areas serving IT equipment, such as switchgear, UPS systems, pumps and cooling plant. Physical boundaries and included systems vary by project.
A project-specific area label. This course’s example uses it for the site and utility interface; other organizations use it for connectivity or broader support areas. Confirm the site definition.
A conductor assembly used to distribute electrical power. In the illustrated Open Rack DC system, it carries DC from the power shelf to compatible equipment; it does not convert AC to DC.
A device that converts alternating current to direct current. Modular rectifiers in a rack power shelf can provide DC to a common rack busbar.

lms_catalog.overview: Discover how everyday digital services depend on computing equipment, networks, electrical power, cooling and physical facilities. Four narrated modules introduce facility types, AI factories and workload placement, availability concepts, power and heat paths, rack DC busbars, rack dimensions and equipment, ownership responsibilities, and resource-efficiency measures. Ten instructional videos are complemented by diagrams, eight narration-timed teaching videos, thirteen knowledge checks with informative feedback, and a glossary. Relevant 2026 OCP publications connect these foundations to shared interfaces and chip-to-grid coordination, with a clear next step into the existing Intro to OCP course series.
